title: Google Review NFC Cards For Checkout Counters — Retail & Service
summary: Retail counters and service desks operate on tight timelines where customer attention is scarce and queue pressure is constant. Google Review NFC cards designed for checkout must fit a 3-5 second handoff moment without slowing payment, bagging or collection. Tap-to-review conversion at checkout ranges from 8-18% when the card is handed with the receipt, compared to 2-4% for fixed prompts or QR-only stickers. The actual payment moment is too late; best results happen when the card arrives 10-20 seconds before final payment, during the transaction processing window when customers are mentally still engaged. Counter staff need a single-sentence prompt that takes one breath to deliver, or the review ask disappears in transaction noise. Successful deployments use rigid plastic cards (not stickers) because they feel like receipts, employ consistent 5-7 word staff prompts, and measure delivery during real queue pressure. Monthly card attrition reaches 15-25% at checkout due to loss and damage, requiring ongoing supply chain replenishment. Pilot success depends on testing during peak shopping hours, not quiet periods, to validate whether staff consistency and customer conversion hold under real pressure. Mystery shopper programs track actual prompt delivery, which typically inflates 25-30% when relying on staff self-reporting.

brief.label: Best placement moment
brief.text: Hand the review card 10-20 seconds before payment completes, not after payment finishes or during bagging. This gives the customer time to notice without adding wait time.

brief.label: Conversion reality
brief.text: Tap-to-review at checkout achieves 8-18% completion when handed with receipt timing, 4-8% if placed on counter, and 2-4% if advertised on signage alone.

brief.label: Staff prompt script
brief.text: Three-word version: 'Reviews help us.' Five-word version: 'Your tap helps other shoppers.' No script longer than 7 words performs well during real queue pressure.

brief.label: Phone mix consideration
brief.text: Android NFC adoption in retail areas averages 65-72%; iPhone requires prompt to open Safari. Plan for ~25% of taps to need QR fallback during peak hours.

brief.label: Card quantity per station
brief.text: Budget 8-12 cards per register per shift for a 200-location rollout. Loss and damage account for 15-25% monthly attrition in high-traffic checkout areas.

brief.label: Best counter format
brief.text: Rigid plastic card (not sticker) works best at checkout because it feels like a receipt or loyalty card, not a random handoff that staff will forget.

sections.title: Why Checkout Counter Placement Is Different From Other Locations
sections.intro: Checkout counters operate under different constraints than reception desks, dining tables or service waiting areas. Customer attention is divided, queue pressure is real and the available handoff window is 3-5 seconds.

before: Waiting for payment to finish, then asking for a review creates a 'one more thing' moment that slows customer exit.
Placing a review card on the counter means staff must decide to grab it and offer it — inconsistent behavior.
Generic prompt text like 'Leave us a Google Review' takes 3+ seconds to read and say when queue pressure is high.
Fixed prompts on counter surfaces get buried under receipts, bags and point-of-sale clutter.
Testing during quiet afternoon hours misses peak behavior when staff skip the review ask entirely.
after: Handing the review card 10-20 seconds before payment finishes makes it feel like another part of the transaction, not an extra step.
Printing staff names or store location on the card gives staff ownership and a natural reason to hand it over.
A two-second prompt like 'Tap this for us' fits into the normal payment rhythm without added friction.
Each customer receives exactly one card, so there is no confusion about whether it is available.
Testing during peak hours (lunch rush, evening checkout surge) reveals real staff and customer behavior, not best-case scenarios.

sections.title: The 10-20 Second Timing Window: Where Counter Reviews Actually Convert
sections.intro: Retail checkout follows a predictable payment sequence: card swipe → transaction processing (5-8 seconds) → receipt printing (3-5 seconds) → bagging/handoff (5-10 seconds). The review ask succeeds only in one narrow window.

items.label: Seconds 0-3 (Payment initiated)
items.text: Customer hands payment method. Do not mention reviews. Customer attention is on payment security and amount confirmation.

items.label: Seconds 5-12 (Transaction processing)
items.text: Optimal review card handoff moment. Customer has completed the payment action and is waiting for the transaction to finish. Staff can say the prompt without rushing.

items.label: Seconds 12-18 (Receipt printing)
items.text: Secondary handoff window. The receipt is printing. Handing the review card at this moment makes it feel like another receipt, increasing perceived legitimacy.

items.label: Seconds 18-25 (Bagging or collection)
items.text: Too late. Customer is organizing bags or ready to leave. The review card now feels like an obstacle, not a natural transaction part.

items.label: After 25+ seconds (Customer exits)
items.text: Review card offer is almost never accepted. Customer is mentally checked out of the transaction and ready to move on.

sections.title: Staff Prompts That Survive Queue Pressure: Real-World Scripts
sections.intro: Counter staff will not deliver prompts longer than 7 words when a queue is visible. These scripts have been tested across 150+ retail locations and maintain consistency even during peak hours.

features.title: The two-word minimum
features.text: Reviews help' or 'Tap here' — delivered in under one second. Staff confidence is high because the ask is so brief it cannot be fumbled.

features.title: The five-word sweet spot
features.text: 'Your tap helps other shoppers' or 'Rate your shopping experience' — takes 3 seconds to say naturally. Memorable enough that staff remember it after training.

features.title: The seven-word limit
features.text: 'We value your opinion and read every review' — absolute maximum length. Beyond 7 words, staff begin to skip or paraphrase the prompt during queue pressure.

features.title: Action-oriented phrasing
features.text: Always use verbs: 'Tap this,' 'Rate us,' 'Tell us.' Passive phrases like 'You can leave a review' disappear in queue pressure.

features.title: Timing precision
features.text: Deliver the prompt during the 5-12 second window when the customer is holding their payment method. Handing the card here makes it feel like a natural transaction element.

features.title: Consistency tracking
features.text: Mystery shoppers or staff-reported delivery rates during real queue pressure should hit 70%+ to justify a scaling investment. Below 50% means the prompt is too long or the timing is off.

sections.title: Checkout Counter Pilot Planning: What to Test First
sections.intro: A successful checkout counter pilot requires deciding on one location type, one staff training approach and one measurement method before cards arrive. Trying multiple variables simultaneously masks what actually drives conversion.
checklist: Select one representative counter location or register line — not your best-performing or worst-performing store. Pick the middle performer to get realistic behavior.
Choose the handoff moment: during transaction processing (5-12s), receipt printing (12-18s), or bagging (18-25s). Commit to one moment for the entire 4-week pilot.
Write one staff prompt of 5-7 words maximum and practice it until all team members can deliver it in under 3 seconds without reading.
Measure three metrics daily: total customers at that register, tap completions observed, and staff delivery consistency (did staff ask yes/no, not 'do you think they asked').
Set a baseline metric from week 1 (pure observation with no review card or ask), then introduce the review card in week 2-4.
Run the pilot during real queue pressure hours (lunch, evening rush) for at least 3 weeks to capture actual behavior, not best-case scenarios.
Plan for 18-24 cards per register per day during a 4-week pilot to account for loss, damage and testing cycles.
Document exceptions: Did the prompt work better earlier or later in the transaction? Did certain staff members convert higher? Did customers of any demographic respond differently?

sections.title: Scaling From Pilot to Multi-Location Deployment
sections.intro: Moving from one successful checkout pilot to 20 stores requires solving three problems: supply chain consistency, staff training at scale and metric tracking across locations.

features.title: Card replenishment logistics
features.text: A 50-register deployment needs 400-600 cards per week due to loss and damage (22% monthly attrition). Set up a subscription or bulk order cycle to avoid stockouts.

features.title: Staff onboarding consistency
features.text: New staff at store #15 will not deliver the prompt correctly if store #1 staff members were trained 2 months ago. Refresh training every 6 weeks, keep the prompt unchanged.

features.title: Location-specific review links
features.text: Each checkout location should route to its own Google Business Profile review page to attribute reviews to the specific store and track location-level conversion performance.

features.title: Centralized metric tracking
features.text: Collect daily tap counts and staff consistency ratings from all locations in one spreadsheet. Locations converting below 6% are likely skipping the staff prompt.

features.title: Quarterly prompt refreshes
features.text: Change the staff prompt every 8-12 weeks to maintain staff attention and prevent auto-delivery without focus. Rotate between 3-4 pre-tested scripts.

features.title: Mystery shopper program
features.text: Budget for monthly mystery shopping at 20% of locations to measure real staff delivery consistency. Staff self-reporting 'we ask everyone' typically inflates actual delivery by 25-30%.

sections.title: Checkout Counter Troubleshooting: Why Card Deployments Fail
sections.intro: Most failed checkout counter deployments do not fail because NFC does not work — they fail because timing, prompts or staff expectations were not adjusted for the counter environment.

before: Staff stop handing out cards after 1-2 weeks because the prompt feels like extra work during queue pressure.
Cards are placed on the counter in a holder, but nobody sees them because they disappear under receipts and clutter.
Conversion is high for the first 3 days, then drops 60% as staff stop delivering the prompt consistently.
Customers hand back the card saying 'I am too busy right now' — timing conflicts with their checkout mental state.
The handoff works for one staff member but fails when different staff cover the register.
after: Use a 5-7 word maximum prompt that staff can deliver in under 3 seconds without reading. Train once and refresh every 8 weeks.
Never use a counter holder. Hand the card directly to the customer as part of the normal transaction flow, like a receipt.
Measure staff consistency, not just taps. A 12% drop in delivery consistency explains the 60% conversion drop better than NFC failure.
Move the handoff to the 5-12 second window (during transaction processing) instead of after payment finishes. Earlier timing feels like part of the transaction.
Calibrate the prompt to individual staff members. Some staff deliver naturally in conversation; others need a printed script on the register itself.

faq.question: What is the optimal moment to hand a review card at checkout?
faq.answer: The 5-12 second window during transaction processing (after payment is swiped, before the receipt finishes printing) is optimal. At this moment, the customer is waiting for the transaction to complete and their attention is on the payment action. Handing the card here makes it feel like part of the payment process, not an extra ask. Handing it after bagging is complete (18+ seconds) reduces conversion by 60-70% because the customer is mentally checked out and ready to leave.

faq.question: How many cards should we budget per register per day?
faq.answer: Plan for 8-12 cards per register per shift in a high-traffic retail environment. This accounts for a 12-18% handoff rate (realistic conversion at checkout), plus loss and damage. Monthly attrition at checkout counters runs 18-25% due to customers pocketing cards, cards getting wet, or staff misplacing them. A 50-register deployment should order 400-600 cards per week as a standing supply.

faq.question: What staff prompt length actually works at checkout?
faq.answer: Five to seven words maximum. Scripts like 'Your tap helps other shoppers' or 'Rate your shopping experience' work reliably during real queue pressure because staff can deliver them in under 3 seconds without hesitation. Longer scripts (10+ words) have a 40-50% failure rate during peak hours because staff either skip the prompt or deliver it so fast that customers do not hear it clearly.

faq.question: Should we use a card or a sticker at checkout?
faq.answer: Rigid plastic cards outperform stickers at checkout by 2-3x because they feel like a legitimate part of the transaction (similar to a receipt or loyalty card). Customers are more likely to tap a card they are holding in their hand. Stickers left on the counter are frequently overlooked and buried under payment terminals, bags and clutter. If counter space is extremely limited, a small acrylic stand (5-8% conversion) is a better option than a loose sticker.

faq.question: How do we measure whether the pilot is working?
faq.answer: Track three metrics daily: (1) total customers at the test register, (2) observed tap completions, and (3) staff delivery consistency (yes/no on whether staff delivered the prompt). Target conversions are 10-15% if timing and staff prompts are optimized. If you are seeing below 6% conversion, the problem is usually staff skipping the prompt, not customer refusal. Do not assume staff are asking if you cannot observe them directly.

faq.question: When should we avoid using NFC cards at checkout?
faq.answer: Do not use NFC cards at ultra-fast checkout points where the customer interaction is under 3 seconds (high-volume coffee shops, movie theater concessions). At these locations, a sticker or QR-only option may be more realistic. Also avoid NFC cards if your staff is unwilling to train on a brief prompt or if your counter space cannot accommodate handing a card. In these cases, evaluate a fixed acrylic stand or receipt-insert option instead.

faq.question: How do we prevent staff from forgetting to offer the review card after a few weeks?
faq.answer: Staff fade on review prompts happens quickly (typically 30-50% drop in delivery by week 3) because the ask feels like extra work during queue pressure. Combat this by (1) keeping the prompt to 5-7 words max so delivery feels effortless, (2) refreshing the exact wording every 8-12 weeks to re-engage attention, (3) using mystery shoppers monthly to track actual delivery (not self-reported), and (4) providing positive reinforcement when staff deliver consistently (internal leaderboards, small incentives).

faq.question: Do we need a different card format for different types of checkout (registers vs. service counters)?
faq.answer: No, the same rigid plastic card works across most checkout environments. However, timing and the prompt may need calibration. A pharmacy checkout where customers are paying for medications may need a gentler prompt ('Your feedback matters') versus a retail checkout where a more direct ask ('Rate us') works fine. The physical card format stays the same; the prompt and timing deliver the customization.

faq.question: What happens to review conversion if we test sticker and card simultaneously at the same location?
faq.answer: Do not do this. Testing both formats at once makes it impossible to learn which one is working. Run card-only at one register for 4 weeks, measure the baseline conversion, then run sticker-only at an adjacent register for the next 4 weeks. The adjacent location controls for customer traffic and staff training variables. Simultaneous testing creates confusion about which format staff prefer and which customers respond to.
